intro: This one's against ChiefRockka — a scrappy game where both of us made some big mistakes, but I managed to hold on and find the checkmate.

lines.text: My opponent plays bishop takes f2, check — a piece sacrifice on move three. Looks scary, but the engine says it's a blunder. I just need to stay calm.
Here my opponent plays c6, locking the knight in. The engine wanted the knight to develop instead — small decisions like this quietly hurt your position.
And here I go and blunder it right back. I play bishop takes f7, check — felt clever, but the engine wanted queen to d3. I got greedy. Plain and simple.
My opponent moves the king to e8 when bishop to e6 was the tougher defence. Sometimes your opponent bails you out — I'll take it, but I won't pretend I earned it.
I play queen to e6, check — and this is a five-pawn swing against me. Rook takes d6 was the clean kill. I was rushing, like sprinting too early in a race and burning out.
King to e8 again — my opponent keeps moving toward the centre instead of away. King to e6 would have made my life much harder. I'm getting lucky here.
Rook to d6 — checkmate. The engine agrees, that's the best move. Feels good to land it cleanly after all that chaos.

outro: The lesson today: I blundered twice and still won because my opponent blundered more. At our level, staying in the game matters. If this felt relatable, hit subscribe — we're climbing together.
